opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question. The core idea behind Genie is that it's a generative interactive environment, so the "interactive" part is really the whole point. We could have just shown videos generated from a prompt, but then it would look a lot like any other video generation model, and you'd lose what's actually novel here, which is that you can step into the world and take actions and the model responds to them frame by frame.

So having a person actually play in these worlds felt like the most direct and honest way to show that. When you see someone pressing, say, left or jump and the character moves accordingly, and the background parallaxes the way you'd expect, that communicates something a static rollout just can't. It shows that the model has learned a controllable latent action space, even though it was trained purely from unlabeled internet videos with no action labels at all. That was one of the things we were most excited about. The model discovered on its own a small set of consistent actions that mean roughly the same thing across very different environments.

There's also a longer-term motivation. A big part of why we care about this is training agents. If you can generate an essentially unlimited variety of interactive worlds, that's a really rich source of experience for embodied agents. But before you hand those worlds to an agent, it's helpful to verify that they're actually playable, that they're consistent and respond sensibly to inputs. Humans are very good judges of that. If a person can sit down and intuitively control a character in a world that was generated from a sketch, or a photo, or even a kid's drawing, that's a pretty strong signal the environment is coherent enough to be useful.

And honestly, it's just fun. Being able to take a drawing and then play inside it captures people's imagination in a way that I think helps convey where this kind of research could go.

r001.rationale: The response describes human inputs and responsive movement, but does not say random action sequences produce visually jittery behavior.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts human play with static video rollouts, but does not identify generating a game tree as an alternative.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the short answer is that human interaction is really the most direct way to show what Genie actually learned. The whole point of the model is that it's an action-controllable world model. It's not just generating a video that plays out on its own. You give it a frame, and then at every step you take an action, and the model responds to that action. If we had only shown rollouts where the model picks its own actions, or where we just played back a sequence, you wouldn't be able to tell whether the controllability was real or whether it was just producing plausible-looking footage.

And the other piece is that the actions Genie learned are latent. We trained on hundreds of thousands of hours of internet videos of 2D platformers, and none of those videos come with action labels. So the model had to discover, in an unsupervised way, a small discrete set of actions that explain how frames change over time. When we first looked at them, we had a hypothesis that they'd correspond to things like move left, move right, jump. But the honest way to verify that is to put a human in the loop, let them press action one, action two, action three, and see whether the behavior is consistent and whether it feels like controlling a character. It turned out that it did, and that consistency held across very different starting images, including sketches and photographs that were nowhere near the training distribution.

There's also a motivational reason. A lot of what excites us about this direction is the idea that anyone could draw a scene or take a picture and then step into it as a playable world. That's inherently an interactive experience. Showing people playing in those worlds just communicated the idea far better than any metric we could have reported. And it also set up the longer-term goal, which is using these environments to train agents. If a human can act in the world and get coherent responses, then an agent can too, and that's the stepping stone toward using Genie-style models as unlimited training environments.

When a person takes an action, the environment needs to respond to that action and generate what happens next. Having a human play makes that distinction really tangible: you can explore, try different things, and see how the world responds.

sol-6.1.text: We wanted to show that these are environments you can actually interact with, rather than just videos you can watch. Having a person control the actions makes that distinction intuitive: you press a button, the world responds, and you can choose what to do next. It’s a direct way to demonstrate the connection between the actions and what Genie generates.
